text: Energy Layer 1 should be treated primarily as electricity-system expansion rather than a generic commodity-energy basket.
Highest-quality first-pass chokepoints are grid transformers, medium-voltage switchgear, substations, transmission/distribution EPC, and mission-critical electrical construction.

Data centers belong in the universe as demand-node validators, but their Serenity score should be below scarce equipment and construction bottlenecks unless powered-capacity pricing evidence is strong.
Nuclear workstream should prioritize fuel-cycle scarcity, HALEU, enrichment, conversion, and long-term contracting before speculative SMR deployment stories.
Gas and LNG names need decomposition into commodity gas, midstream constraints, LNG export capacity, gas turbines, on-site generation, and dispatchable power economics.
Layer 2 must add company-specific evidence for non-visible candidates, especially Eaton, Quanta, GE Vernova, Constellation, BWXT, Cameco, Cheniere, midstream gas names, storage, and renewables.
Deduplication retained one active CEG candidate; future pipeline should enforce ticker uniqueness before scoring to avoid duplicate rows.

Highest-priority Energy chokepoint is grid deliverability, especially large power transformers, distribution transformers, substations, switchgear, and transmission interconnection rather than generic electricity demand alone.

AI/data-center load is the dominant demand driver to track, but Serenity mapping should also include industrial manufacturing load, LNG/gas demand, electrification, and local permitting as interacting drivers.
Track PJM/FERC large-load, co-location, price-collar, expedited interconnection, and backstop procurement actions as near-term regulatory catalysts.
Track earnings disclosures from electrical-equipment and gas-turbine suppliers for backlog, book-to-bill, lead times, data-center order mix, and capacity-expansion plans.

Next layer should verify company-specific exposure for Layer 1 candidates: data-center/grid revenue mix, backlog quality, customer concentration, margin durability, capacity additions, and whether current valuation already prices the bottleneck.
Need region-by-region validation for ERCOT, PJM, SERC/Southeast, WECC, and MISO because load growth, market design, interconnection rules, fuel constraints, and rate treatment differ materially.

POWL is a direct electrical-equipment chokepoint candidate for AI/data-center power delivery via engineered switchgear, control, and distribution systems; evidence is strong on backlog but needs end-market mix and lead-time validation.

HUBB is a utility-grid infrastructure supplier mapped to T&D, substation, grid hardening, and electrical-solutions demand; relationship strength depends on utility capex and substation order evidence.

FIX is a high-quality mission-critical construction execution candidate because backlog growth and company disclosures point to strong technology/data-center demand, including modular and electrical operations.
STRL maps to data-center site development and E-Infrastructure rather than equipment scarcity; verify data-center concentration and acquired electrical/mechanical revenue contribution.
EME maps to electrical and mechanical construction labor/execution for data centers and network/communications projects; must separate organic demand from Miller Electric acquisition contribution.
IESC maps to specialized electrical and communications installation for data centers, with record Communications backlog and favorable large data-center project execution disclosed in fiscal 2025.

D is a regulated-utility expression of Northern Virginia/PJM DOM data-center load growth; upside and risk depend heavily on Virginia SCC rate treatment, large-load tariffs, IRP approvals, and bill backlash.
NVT is a component-level data-center and utility infrastructure supplier; current evidence supports exposure but not yet hard bottleneck control.

VST is a firm-power scarcity candidate through nuclear and gas generation in constrained power markets, with a material Meta PPA disclosed for PJM nuclear output; relationship remains sensitive to market rules, hedging, and regulatory outcomes.

EQIX and DLR are demand-side data-center platforms; they validate the load-growth theme but may be beneficiaries or cost bearers depending on power procurement, lease pricing, capex inflation, and interconnection access.

CMI maps directly to backup and on-site data-center power through generators, controls, paralleling systems, transfer switches, and generator technologies; emissions rules and competition are key falsification vectors.

Need market-pricing layer before any ranking upgrade: valuation, revenue exposure, backlog quality, margin normalization, order conversion, customer concentration, capex needs, balance sheet pressure, and crowding/short-interest checks for all tickers.
Need primary-source filings for NVT with explicit data-center and power-utility revenue mix; current relationship evidence is less specific than for POWL, FIX, CMI, EME, IESC, and STRL.

Need regional mapping between PJM, ERCOT, Virginia, Texas, Georgia, Pennsylvania, and other data-center hot spots to distinguish utilities, contractors, and suppliers with local exposure from generic electrification beta.

ETN should be tracked as a broad electrical-equipment/data-center power distribution beneficiary; key Serenity evidence variables are Electrical backlog, book-to-bill, data-center order mix, lead times, and margin expansion.
PWR is one of the cleanest public mappings to the grid EPC and skilled-labor bottleneck; 2025 record total backlog and Electric segment backlog support upgrading evidence quality.
GEV spans dispatchable generation equipment and grid equipment; gas turbine slot reservations and grid-product order growth are the main Layer 3 validation fields.
CEG has direct evidence for hyperscaler nuclear demand through the Microsoft 20-year Crane Clean Energy Center PPA; key risk is restart/regulatory/capex execution rather than thematic relevance.
LEU is the most direct public-market mapping in this chunk to the HALEU bottleneck, but contract/task-order funding and production scale remain the key falsification variables.
CCJ maps to uranium, UF6 conversion, fuel services, and Westinghouse; evidence is strong for nuclear fuel-cycle exposure but less direct for AI/data-center power demand.
SO has concrete Southeast load-growth evidence tied to data centers and advanced manufacturing; economics should be validated through IRPs, rate cases, and large-load contract structures.
PCG has data-center load evidence but should be kept in a regulatory-risk bucket because wildfire liabilities, affordability, and CPUC cost recovery can dominate the load-growth thesis.
NEE and AES are renewables/storage PPA mappings; Serenity priority should depend on interconnection-ready contracted backlog and data-center customer exposure, not broad renewables exposure.

Need a current Layer 3 market-pricing check for all names: valuation versus normalized earnings, backlog-to-revenue conversion, crowding, short interest, customer concentration, and whether AI-power exposure is already priced in.
Need company-level 2026 updates for all tickers because the Energy/data-center power theme is moving quickly and backlog, capacity, contract, and regulatory facts may change quarter to quarter.

Within the LNG/midstream part of the candidate chunk, WMB and ET have the clearest data-center/power-demand relationships because they disclose specific data-center or power-plant gas capacity projects and long-duration demand-pull contracts.
KMI is relevant to data-center power demand through gas-pipeline infrastructure but currently needs more customer/project-level evidence than WMB and ET before being upgraded in the Serenity funnel.

LNG is a global LNG export and gas-demand proxy, not a direct AI data-center power-delivery chokepoint; monitor whether U.S. domestic gas demand tightens feedgas costs or improves LNG contracting power.
FSLR has credible domestic solar manufacturing/backlog exposure, but the Serenity chokepoint remains downstream interconnection, transmission, storage, and firm capacity rather than modules alone.
FLNC maps to a plausible grid-flexibility chokepoint, but backlog-to-margin conversion and battery supply-chain risk are the decisive next validation points.

ENPH is lower priority for the AI/data-center power chokepoint because current evidence is dominated by residential solar cyclicality and U.S. policy headwinds; upgrade only if grid-edge/VPP or commercial storage evidence becomes material.
FCX and SCCO should be treated as broad copper commodity proxies for grid/electrification capex; Serenity validation requires copper market-pricing, supply-cost, and jurisdictional risk checks.
MP is strategically relevant to domestic rare earth magnets but is less direct to the immediate grid/data-center power chokepoint than natural-gas delivery, transformers, switchgear, and storage.

Need comparable valuation/crowding check across WMB, ET, KMI, LNG, FSLR, ENPH, FLNC, FCX, SCCO, and MP before any Layer 3 prioritization; this layer maps relationships only and does not make buy/sell recommendations.

Need standardized company-level metrics: percentage of EBITDA/revenue tied to target node, backlog/book-to-bill, contract duration, capex remaining, in-service schedule, regulatory risk, and margin sensitivity.
